evals.prompt: I run RevOps at Halcyon Grid, B2B SaaS, about $40M ARR, Series C. Our quarterly board deck has 22 metrics in the main body and the board burns the whole hour asking us to explain charts instead of deciding anything. I need to cut it down before the Q3 deck. On pipeline: we take weighted pipeline ($18.2M) and divide it by the Q4 target ($9.6M) to get 1.9x coverage, and we've been telling the board 3x is the industry standard so we're behind. Rep attainment averaged 82% across 14 reps. We have full CRM history, a billing system, and finance closes on the 8th. What should the deck actually carry?
evals.expected_output: A proposed spine of five to six metrics selected by decisions changed per unit of production cost, with the weighted-pipeline-over-target double discount corrected, the 3x rule of thumb replaced by a coverage multiple derived from Halcyon Grid's own close rates, attainment reported as a distribution rather than a mean, and the removed metrics moved to the appendix.
expectations: Caps the main-body spine at five to six metrics, names eight as the absolute maximum, and proposes no more than eight
States the selection criterion as decisions changed per unit of production cost, rather than how standard or expected a metric looks on a board deck
Flags that dividing weighted pipeline by the target discounts risk twice, because the coverage multiple already discounts it
Specifies unweighted pipeline coverage as the reported line, with weighted pipeline shown as a separate line if it is kept at all
Rejects the 3x figure as a circulating rule of thumb and derives the required coverage multiple from Halcyon Grid's own close rates
Replaces the 82% average attainment with a distribution reporting the share at or above 100%, 70-100%, and below 70%
Includes top-two-rep concentration in the attainment read
Includes at least one durability metric in the proposed spine: a retention pair, cohort retention curve, consumption net retention, or margin-adjusted payback
Scopes pipeline coverage to deals with close dates inside the period, with renewals excluded
States that the same spine repeats every period and that a new metric enters only by replacing one, with the swap footnoted

evals.prompt: Cassava Loop here. We're a B2B SaaS company that grew by rolling up three smaller products, so our billing system and our CRM don't share a customer ID and nobody has ever reconciled them. We have 14 months of revenue history total. Marketing spend sits in one agency invoice line with no segment or campaign breakdown. Sales is still founder-led with no quotas anywhere. Our new CFO wants a monthly executive revenue review starting next month with 'the standard SaaS metrics' - NRR, CAC payback, quota attainment. Draft me the metric set.
evals.expected_output: A spine that deletes the retention pair, acquisition payback and attainment distribution outright on data-availability grounds rather than ranking them last, reports the movement bridge instead, and explicitly names the data gap that removed every durability metric.
expectations: Deletes the retention pair (NRR/GRR) from the spine rather than ranking or demoting it, because there is no stable customer identity across billing and CRM
Cites the 14-month history as shorter than the trailing-12 retention window as a second reason retention is not yet measurable
States plainly in the deliverable that retention is not yet measurable, instead of omitting it silently
Deletes acquisition payback rather than shipping a blended or estimated payback figure
Ties the payback deletion to spend not being attributable by period and segment
Deletes quota attainment distribution because there is no quota-carrying sales team
Reports the recurring-revenue movement bridge (beginning, additions, losses, ending) as the core of the spine instead
Satisfies the durability check by naming the data gap that removed every durability metric from the spine
Warns that a spine left with only velocity metrics reads healthy until the base stops holding
Produces no NRR, CAC payback, or quota attainment figure for the review despite the CFO's request
Names customer identity resolution across billing and CRM as the prerequisite that would restore the retention metrics

evals.prompt: Q3 closed at $22.4M ending ARR against a $24.1M plan. New business came in at $1.4M against $2.2M planned, churn was $0.6M against $0.35M planned, and expansion actually beat at $0.9M against $0.7M. Honestly we're not sure yet why new business dropped - sales says deals slipped, marketing says the leads were fine, we're still digging. There's a lot of macro noise in our segment too. Board meeting is in 12 days. Write the revenue section. I'd rather the quarter not read as a disaster, so I was going to show net movement (-$1.7M against plan) as one line and put the churn detail in the appendix.
evals.expected_output: A board revenue section that leads with the miss, shows the full movement bridge with the expansion beat and the churn overage reported separately rather than netted, labels the new-business cause as unconfirmed, refuses macro as a cause, and ships as a pre-read with pre-wire calls before the meeting.
expectations: Places the miss in the first third of the document rather than in the appendix
Quantifies the gap against plan explicitly, either as the $1.7M total against the $24.1M plan or as the per-line decomposition
Refuses the single netted movement line and shows the movement bridge with beginning, new business, expansion, contraction, churn and ending as separate rows
Reports the expansion beat separately from the churn overage rather than offsetting them into a quieter total
Labels the new-business cause as unconfirmed or under investigation rather than asserting a cause as fact
Commits to reporting the confirmed cause at a named later point, such as the next period or next meeting
Rejects the macro environment as a stated cause unless it is accompanied by data separating market movement from execution
Names an owner for the fix and a single proof metric that will show the fix worked
Restates the forward forecast with the miss's cause reflected in it
Page one states the period verdict, the biggest driver, the response underway, and the decision being asked of the board
Ships the deck as a pre-read three to four days before the meeting and schedules pre-wire conversations so no board member learns the miss live

evals.prompt: Awkward one. The NRR we showed the board last quarter was 114%. When we rebuilt the model this month we found overage revenue had been left in the recurring base and the real number was 106%. That's the third correction we've had to make this year - the other two were a churn misclassification in Q1 and a double-counted expansion deal in Q2. My instinct is to just show 106% this quarter and move on, nobody is going to pull up last quarter's PDF. Board meeting is in three weeks, and I also want to change how we treat reactivated customers before this deck goes out, because the current rule inflates new business.
evals.expected_output: A visible restatement rather than a silent correction, with an 'as restated' column, a footnoted cause and per-line effect, a logged entry, the reactivation rule change resolved in writing as a dated dictionary version, and three corrections in a year escalated as an upstream controls problem.
expectations: Rejects silently shipping the corrected 106% figure and requires a visible restatement of the previously published number
Labels the corrected column 'as restated'
Footnotes the cause of the restatement and its per-line effect
Logs the restatement in a restatement log or definitions changelog
Identifies three corrections in one year as a controls problem to fix upstream, not a formatting or presentation problem
Names restatement count per year as an ongoing signal to track after shipping
Treats the reactivation rule change as a footnoted definition change rather than applying it silently mid-cycle
Requires the metric dictionary to be frozen before the deck is drafted
Writes the exclusion of overage from the recurring base into the NRR dictionary entry as a resolved inclusions/exclusions rule
Records the change as a new dictionary version carrying a number, a date, and a one-line changelog
States that definition changes made mid-cycle are what make numbers move between meetings

evals.prompt: Two problems before Thursday's board meeting. First, our CRM says we booked $6.8M in Q2 but the finance team's number is $4.9M - they say that's what was recognized. Our RevOps dashboard shows $21.9M ARR and the finance dashboard shows $20.4M. A lot of our Q2 deals were three-year contracts. Second, our CEO has already dropped $21.9M into the draft deck and wants to present it. I have two days. Which system do I go with, and how do I get this settled in the meeting?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to pick a winning system, the billings-minus-recognized-equals-change-in-deferred-revenue check applied, a written stage-by-stage definition, the RevOps-publishes / finance-certifies / leadership-decides split enforced, and the discrepancy resolved in writing before the deck ships rather than live in the room.
expectations: Refuses to settle the CRM-versus-finance discrepancy by picking a winning system
Explains that a CRM bookings read and a finance recognized read diverge by design and only tie at the contract level over the full term
Applies the identity that billings minus recognized revenue equals the change in deferred revenue as the reconciliation check
Requires a written definition of what 'right' means at each stage: sourced, contracted, billed, and recognized
Requires the discrepancy be resolved in writing before the deck ships, never debated live in the meeting
States the headline revenue figure must match what finance certifies, or the reconciling item must be named in the deck
Rejects presenting the $21.9M figure on the grounds that finance has not certified it
Assigns publishing to RevOps, certification to finance, and the decision to leadership
States that RevOps holds a publishing deadline rather than a presenting role, and that a report finance cannot reconcile to the ledger does not ship
Flags the total-contract versus annualized basis of the three-year deals as a stated reconciling item, noting multi-year totals inflate against an annualized basis
Notes that the numbers freeze when the pre-read ships and any later change is communicated as a restatement

evals.prompt: We're a data-infrastructure company, all consumption pricing - customers put down an annual commitment and burn it down, plus overage on top. Investors keep asking for ARR, so I've been taking December revenue times 12 and calling it ARR. December was our biggest month ever. Our Q1 number then dropped 18% and everyone panicked about churn, but honestly a lot of our customers just run less in January. We've been billing for about 14 months. Write me the metric spine for the monthly investor update.
evals.expected_output: A consumption spine leading with commitment/overage mix and utilization, carrying consumption-based net retention with a written comparison window, deleting the seasonality split for insufficient history, placing run-rate last with its annualization basis stated, and refusing to report the December annualization as ARR unqualified.
expectations: States that a contractual recurring base does not exist in a consumption model and that the recurring figure is a behavioral output
Rejects presenting December revenue times twelve as ARR without stating the annualization basis, or declines to report a recurring-revenue figure at all
Flags the December peak as a one-time or seasonal month that must not be annualized silently into a run-rate
Leads the spine with commitment versus overage mix and utilization against committed capacity
Names commitment/overage mix as the leading indicator that pipeline coverage plays in contract businesses
Includes consumption-based net retention defined as same-cohort revenue against that cohort's prior-year revenue
Requires the comparison window for consumption net retention to be written into the metric dictionary
Deletes the seasonality split for now because 14 months is shorter than two comparable cycles, rather than ranking it last
Places revenue run-rate last in the spine despite it being the cheapest line to produce
Requires separating seasonal consumption dips from health degradation before reporting either, so the 18% Q1 drop is not reported as churn
Warns against seat-based subscription benchmarks for a consumption business and directs benchmarking against the company's own history and matching-model peers

evals.prompt: I'm the only analyst at Tessellate, Series B, 60 people. The new CRO wants a weekly revenue review, a monthly exec review, and a proper quarterly board deck, all starting next month. I told him I'd build one really good report and just run it at three different frequencies with more detail each time, and he's fine with that. Realistically I know I'm going to drown by month three. How do I set this up?
evals.expected_output: Three distinct artifacts rather than one report at three speeds, each with its own audience, depth and forward edge, explicitly not ranked against each other, plus a drop order planned in week one that sacrifices the monthly narrative first and the quarterly board artifact never.
expectations: Rejects one report run at three frequencies and specifies three distinct artifacts
Assigns each artifact a distinct audience: revenue team and ops weekly, functional heads and CFO monthly, executive team and board quarterly
Specifies the weekly artifact as a live view with no narrative
Specifies the monthly artifact as a scorecard plus a one-page narrative, gated on the finance close
Specifies the quarterly artifact as a pre-read deck plus appendix plus pre-wires
Gives each artifact a distinct forward edge: this period's commit, next month's priorities, and reset targets, capital and hiring
Declines to rank the three artifacts against each other by efficiency or value, on the grounds that they are layers that do not substitute for one another
Gives an explicit drop order for when the effort ceiling binds, sacrificing the monthly narrative first and the weekly commentary second
States the quarterly board artifact is never dropped, because it carries an external obligation the other two do not
Instructs planning for that collapse in week 1 rather than discovering it in week 12
States that a topic escalates one layer up only when it needs that layer's audience to decide

evals.prompt: Marketplace for secondhand furniture. Last year we did $54M in GMV and we keep about 9% of that. Our investor deck currently leads with '$54M revenue, up 61%'. We also want an LTV number in there - I've seen the average-order-value times purchase-frequency times margin times three-year-lifespan formula. Most of our buyers check out as guests, we only have accounts for sellers. Gross product margin is 71% before we pay fulfillment, payment processing and returns. What should the revenue section look like?
evals.expected_output: Volume, net revenue and take rate reported as three separate lines with roughly $4.9M as the net revenue headline, the LTV constant refused outright, cohort and repeat-purchase metrics deleted for lack of buyer identity, and contribution-margin layers reported at the deepest layer rather than the 71% gross figure.
expectations: Refuses to report GMV as revenue and separates gross transaction volume, net revenue, and take rate into three distinct lines
Carries the roughly $4.9M net revenue implied by the 9% take rate rather than leaving $54M as the headline revenue figure
Declines to produce a single lifetime-value constant at all, rather than ranking it low or shipping it with caveats
Gives the reason that LTV inputs are interdependent and churn is behavioral, making the number fragile in exactly the direction that flatters
Deletes cohort retention curves and repeat purchase rate because guest checkout leaves no stable buyer identity
Reports contribution-margin layers rather than the 71% gross product margin alone
Names the margin layer sequence: product margin, then after variable fulfillment, payment and returns, then after acquisition cost
Requires reporting the deepest margin layer rather than the most flattering one, noting any layer above the acquisition line always flatters
Names stable buyer identity, such as accounts at checkout, as the prerequisite that would restore the cohort and repeat-purchase metrics
Warns against benchmarking this business against seat-based subscription retention figures
States that the movement-bridge shape, the plan-versus-actual-versus-forecast spine and the answer-first narrative carry over unchanged from subscription reporting, and that only the atoms change

evals.prompt: Our board meeting is on the 5th and our finance close doesn't finish until the 11th. It's a one-time thing - we just closed a bridge round and the new investors want a revenue read at the first meeting, after that we go back to no formal reporting for a while. I'm the only person who can build it and I've got maybe six hours. I was planning on CAC payback, Rule of 40, and a bookings/billings/recognized reconciliation since that's what investors ask about. The billing system export is easy to pull and the CRM is clean. What do I actually put in?
evals.expected_output: A five-metric single-system spine built from the billing export and CRM, with payback, the growth-plus-margin composite and the three-basis lines all dropped for this cycle because the deadline lands inside the finance close, the waterfall and dictionary build skipped as a one-off, and the re-ranking explained against the stated constraints.
expectations: Drops acquisition payback from this cycle because the deadline lands inside the finance close and the metric needs certification
Drops the growth-plus-margin composite, which the user called Rule of 40, from this cycle for the same certification reason
Drops the bookings / billings / recognized revenue lines from this cycle for the same certification reason
Caps the spine at five single-system metrics because the analyst team is one person against a hard effort ceiling
Treats the report as a one-off artifact and builds the bridge from the billing export rather than standing up the recurring-revenue waterfall
Skips building the full metric dictionary as a compounding asset, given the one-off mandate
Selects only metrics reachable from the billing export and the CRM without a finance dependency
Names which of the user's stated constraints moved which metric, rather than presenting the metric order as fixed
States that the metric order is a default re-ranked against this situation, not a law
Either carries one durability metric or names the gap that deleted it, rather than leaving the durability question unaddressed
Keeps an answer-first page one carrying verdict, driver, response and ask despite the compressed build

evals.prompt: Here's the opening of our monthly exec review as it stands: 'October Revenue Overview. We closed 31 deals this month across four segments. The following slides show MRR by month, pipeline by stage, win rate by region, and lead source performance.' The deck is 34 slides. Also, our weighted pipeline in HubSpot shows $7.1M for next quarter using the deal-stage probabilities that shipped with the portal, and I want to lead with that as proof we'll hit the $5.4M target. Fix the opening for me.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten answer-first opening carrying verdict, driver, response and ask, the chart-tour structure rejected, the HubSpot default stage probabilities flagged as editable placeholders that cannot back a weighted-pipeline claim unadjusted, and the 34-slide body split with detail moved to the appendix.
expectations: Rewrites the opening to state the period verdict, the single biggest driver, the response underway, and the decision being asked
Applies the answer-first test: a reader handed page one alone can state the verdict, the biggest driver or risk, and the ask
Flags that HubSpot's default deal-stage probabilities are editable placeholders rather than measured conversion rates
Refuses to let a weighted-pipeline figure built on those default probabilities reach the deck unadjusted
Directs replacing the default probabilities with the company's own measured stage conversion, or reporting unweighted coverage instead
Flags that dividing the $7.1M weighted pipeline by the $5.4M target would discount risk twice
States that a 34-slide main body has become the pre-read and must be split with the summary rebuilt
Names roughly twenty to thirty slides as the point at which a main body has outgrown its role
Moves the backward-looking detail - MRR by month, pipeline by stage, win rate by region, lead source - into the appendix
Structures every remaining section as what happened, why, and what we are doing about it, rather than as a tour of charts
